newsitem.title: USA: California economy to continue to grow - report.
newsitem.headline: California economy to continue to grow - report.

text.p: California will be a bright spot in the national economy in 1997, with gains forecast in employment and exports, according to a Bank of America report released Tuesday.

In the report, Howard Roth, vice president and director of regional economics at Bank of America, said unemployment in the state continues to fall. California's unemployment rate was 6.9 percent in October 1996, down from 7.8 percent a year earlier, and the lowest rate since December 1990.

While the state's unemployment rate remains considerably higher than the national rate, the gap between the two narrowed in the last year. Unemployment should fall further in 1997, the report projected.
Jobs have grown quickly in several industries, including computer services, biotechnology, film production and electronic component manufacturing, the report stated.

After advancing only 2.4 percent in 1993 and 3.1 percent in 1994, personal income grew 6.2 percent in the state in 1995 and 7.6 percent in first half 1996, giving Californians more to spend. Roth said strong growth in personal income should continue in 1997.
The fiscal health of the state has improved considerably, according to the report. The improving state economy has stimulated state government tax revenues, making the state budget easier to balance.
Roth said, however, that several factors could dampen the California economy in 1997, including an increase in consumer debt, higher interest rates and county fiscal problems.
"The state's deep recession and a shifting of some responsibilities by state government to the counties has created difficult budgetary problems for some county governments," the report pointed out.
Recently passed federal welfare reform will burden county governments that try to offset declines in social welfare spending by state government, the report stated.
Roth said a national recession could also dampen California's growth.

"More than anything, California's economic prospects depend on the continued growth of the national economy," the report said. "Fortunately, the national economy appears to be quite healthy, with remarkably few imbalances after more than five years of growth."
